audience: Intelligent engineers new to relational databases
purpose: The introduction gives a useful relational mental model and judgement about an application lifecycle and first system choice. The collection takes the reader towards expert practice; deeper articles own working depth.
outcomes: The reader understands what a relational database helps an application do and has a concrete reason to learn about it.
The reader can read a table, explain its rows and columns, follow related facts through identifiers, and understand why a current offered price and a price agreed on an order are different facts.

The reader understands how SQL asks for a result from stored facts, can follow a small useful query and its answer, and recognises that combining related rows can change what each result row represents.

The reader can explain why simultaneous purchases can violate a stock rule, how a transaction and a deliberate change protocol protect a business decision, and what a successful commit does and does not establish.

The reader understands that the engine chooses work to answer a query, can distinguish doing less work from waiting, and has a useful first mental model of access paths, memory and recoverable commit.

The reader can distinguish a successful database transaction from a successful application request, including uncertainty after a lost reply, and identify the application responsibilities that remain.
The reader can distinguish crash recovery, failover and restoring an earlier state, and understands the need for an owner, recovery objectives and a tested restore.
The reader understands the application-visible reasons to copy or divide data across servers, including freshness, routing and coordination.

The reader can make a defensible first shortlist among embedded, conventional server and distributed relational arrangements, explain when the choice changes for a reporting or mixed workload, and identify useful evidence and deeper reading for the next decision.

child_scopes.title: Designing relational data
child_scopes.brief: Turn business facts and invariants into relational schemas that remain understandable as requirements change. Develop an order-reservation design from statements of fact through keys, relationships, dependencies, types and constraints, then challenge it with changes, missing values, history and competing writers. The reader should be able to explain what each row means, what identifies it, which invalid states the database rejects, which rules require a transaction protocol, and what a deliberate duplication costs. Own schema meaning and integrity design; SQL owns statement semantics, transactions owns concurrency protocols, application engineering owns delivery of schema and data migrations, and execution owns physical tuning.

child_scopes.title: Working with SQL
child_scopes.brief: Teach a newcomer to read, write and check useful SQL against a small order schema, progressing from an explicit result contract to joins, grouped results and bounded changes. Use PostgreSQL 18 as one executable reference dialect, with a resettable fixture and expected results; label extensions and differences that change the answer rather than running parallel product tutorials. Develop judgement about row grain, duplicate multiplicity, missing values, ties and the rows a statement affects. Introduce substantial query composition and data-change semantics here, with two focused descendants supplying their working depth. Keep views, routines, triggers and import/export statement effects in this article. Own statement meaning and result validation; schema integrity design, transaction protocols, client integration, execution diagnosis and operational procedures have separate owners. Stop when the reader can produce and challenge a query or change against an explicit contract, identify dialect assumptions and choose the relevant depth.

child_scopes.title: Reasoning about transactions
child_scopes.brief: Teach how to turn an application invariant into a transaction protocol whose permitted outcomes can be explained and tested. Use a stock reservation as the running example, using PostgreSQL 18 as the reference engine and SQL dialect, then expose the limits of single-row reasoning with a rule spanning several rows. Connect atomicity, isolation and durability to outcomes; explain snapshots, locks, multiversion concurrency, anomalies, serialisability, conditional changes, uniqueness, deadlocks and retries. Compare named engine contracts where they change the protocol, rather than treating isolation labels as interchangeable. The reader should leave able to analyse a two-session history, choose and justify a protection mechanism, recognise abort and retry boundaries, and design a deterministic concurrency test. The child develops complete multi-row protocols. Application engineering owns connection lifetimes, ambiguous client outcomes, idempotency across requests and external effects; execution owns physical recovery and performance investigation; distribution owns cross-server consistency and transaction coordination.

child_scopes.title: Understanding and improving database work
child_scopes.brief: Build a practical model of the work a relational engine performs, then use it to improve transactional, analytical and mixed workloads. Follow an order lookup, reservation update and sales report through storage, access paths, planning, execution and commit. Give newcomers a first useful diagnosis before directing them to deeper mechanisms and investigation. Distinguish doing less work from waiting less and adding resources; require evidence that an improvement survives representative concurrency and preserves correctness. Own engine mechanisms and performance investigation. Refer transaction correctness, application protocols, service objectives and recovery procedures, and multi-server coordination to their neighbouring articles.

child_scopes.title: Building applications with a relational database
child_scopes.brief: Teach how application boundaries turn database guarantees into reliable product behaviour. Follow an order reservation from a client request through a driver, a bounded transaction and a committed result to confirmation delivery. Give a compact working contract for resource use, result interpretation, retries, external effects and change delivery, then provide focused routes to working depth. Include database-resident behaviour, real-engine tests and bulk data movement. Own client and delivery protocols; use SQL and transaction guarantees supplied by neighbouring articles without reteaching their semantics or mechanisms.

child_scopes.title: Operating and recovering a relational service
child_scopes.topic: Relational service operations, security and recovery
child_scopes.brief: Turn workload, trust and recovery requirements into a service that can be established, observed, changed and recovered deliberately. Follow the same order-reservation service through provisioning, a busy trading period, routine maintenance and an incident. Update one compact service record throughout: illustrative objective values and accepted reservation markers lead to tested settings, before/after observations and a failed acceptance result that forces a policy revision. Label illustrative inputs, modelled outcomes and observed execution distinctly. Teach operational decisions and executable runbooks, using a pinned PostgreSQL release for concrete examples and identifying managed-service substitutions. Engine diagnosis belongs to execution and replication, fencing and routing guarantees belong to distribution; use those mechanisms as preconditions rather than teaching them again. A reader should finish with an owned service specification, actionable alerts, a rehearsed change procedure and evidence that a chosen recovery path meets its objectives.

child_scopes.title: Relational data across servers
child_scopes.topic: Replication and distribution in relational databases
child_scopes.brief: Teach how independently failing relational servers change the database contract. Begin with an order reservation whose writer fails after acknowledging a commit, and whose next read reaches another server. Use operation histories to distinguish replication, partitioning and distributed coordination, then compare a single writer with replicas, application-managed shards and an integrated distributed relational system against an explicit workload and failure budget. Explain enough log, quorum, placement and routing mechanics to choose a path and recognise a broken promise; the three deeper articles supply implementation and operational depth. Keep local transaction semantics with the transactions article and service-wide recovery procedures and backup policy with operations. Teach required distributed-systems reasoning here without depending on a separate programme.
